title: Components in a Graph
directAnswer: Group the nodes that appear in edges into connected components and report the smallest and largest component sizes (only components with at least two nodes count). Union each edge's endpoints with Union-Find, carry a size on every root, then sweep the roots for the min and max size. O(E · α(N)).

remember.pattern: Union-Find component sizing, then min/max over roots
rules: Only components with **≥ 2 nodes** count — every node here appears in some edge, so each component already has at least 2.
Keep a `size` array updated **only on merges**, and read it **only at roots** — non-roots hold stale sizes.
The graph is bipartite (left labels `1..N`, right labels `N+1..2N`), but Union-Find does not care about sides — it just merges labels.
Use **path compression + union by rank** so each operation is `O(α(N))`, effectively constant.
`find` climbs parents in a loop — iterative, so a long chain cannot overflow the call stack.
whenToUse: You only need component **sizes or membership**, not paths or distances
Edges arrive as a flat list and you merge groups incrementally
Bipartite or general undirected graphs where sides are irrelevant to connectivity
antiSignals: You need shortest paths or distances → BFS/Dijkstra, not Union-Find
You must enumerate the actual members of each component → DFS/BFS flood fill is more natural
Edges are removed over time → Union-Find does not support deletion cleanly
You need the bipartite structure itself (2-coloring) → bipartite check, not sizing
remember.takeaway: Union-Find turns a flat edge list into component sizes in near-constant time per edge. Carry the size on the root during merges, then a single sweep over roots gives any aggregate you need — here the smallest and largest.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you reach for Union-Find with size tracking on a connectivity-only question, read sizes only at roots, and correctly aggregate the min and max across components.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Reading the size array at a non-root node (stale value), counting isolated nodes that should be excluded, or initializing 'smallest' to 0 so it never updates.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Maintain size on merge, sweep only roots, seed smallest to +infinity, and note that the bipartite labeling is irrelevant to the merging — it is just an undirected graph.

problemStatement:
There are `2 × N` nodes in an undirected graph, labeled `1` to `2N`. Each edge connects a node from the left set (`1..N`) to a node from the right set (`N+1..2N`). You are given a list of `edges`.

Return two values: the size of the **smallest** connected component and the size of the **largest** connected component, considering only components that contain at least two nodes.
constraints: Each edge's left endpoint is in 1..N, right endpoint in N+1..2N
The graph is undirected; isolated nodes (in no edge) are ignored
At least one edge exists, so at least one component of size ≥ 2 exists
understanding: Every edge ties a left node to a right node, so any node that appears in an edge belongs to a component of size at least two. Nodes that never appear in any edge are alone and excluded. The task is purely about connectivity sizes: merge endpoints into groups, measure each group, and report the extremes. The left/right (bipartite) split is a labeling detail — connectivity merging ignores it entirely.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do isolated nodes count as size-1 components?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. The problem only considers components with at least two nodes, and every node in an edge is already in one. Untouched labels are ignored.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the bipartite structure matter to the algorithm?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Not for sizing. Union-Find merges whatever labels an edge connects; the left/right split is irrelevant to connected components.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the same edge appear twice?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, and it is harmless — a union whose endpoints already share a root does nothing.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could there be a single giant component?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — then smallest and largest are equal. Seed smallest to infinity so a lone component still sets both.

examples.explanation: Edge 2–6 links the {1,6} and {2,7} groups into {1,2,6,7} (size 4). {3,8} and {4,9} stay size 2. Smallest 2, largest 4.
{1,5,6} has size 3, {2,4} has size 2. Smallest 2, largest 3.
A single component of size 2 — smallest and largest coincide.

diagrams.caption: Sizes-and-membership only, with an incremental edge list, points to Union-Find.

approaches.name: DFS / BFS Flood Fill (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: A natural first take: build an adjacency list, flood-fill each unvisited node to measure its component, and track the min and max sizes. Correct and intuitive.
hints: What do you need per component? Just its node count. How do you count every node reachable from a start?
Build an adjacency list, then walk each unvisited node, flood-filling its whole component and counting how many nodes it touches.
Track the smallest and largest counts among components with size ≥ 2 as you discover them.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Building the adjacency list is O(V + E). Each node and edge is visited once during the flood fills → O(V + E). Tracking min/max is O(1) per component.
approaches.explanation:
If the only quantity you need is each component's size, a flood fill delivers it directly.

**Why flood fill works.** Start at any unvisited node and walk every node reachable through edges, marking visited and counting. When the walk stalls you have one full component and its exact size. Move to the next unvisited node and repeat. Each node is counted once, so the sizes partition every node that has an edge.

**Why iterate over only the nodes in edges.** Untouched labels are isolated and excluded by the problem, so it is cleanest to seed flood fills from nodes that actually appear in an edge (or to skip any component of size 1 when aggregating).

**Why the traversal must be iterative.** With up to `3 × 10⁴` labels and `10⁵` edges, a component can be a long chain. A recursive DFS would nest one frame per node and risk a stack overflow, so use an explicit stack or a BFS queue. Order does not affect the sizes.

**Aggregating extremes.** Keep `smallest` (seeded to infinity) and `largest` (seeded to 0). For each component of size `s ≥ 2`, update both. Seeding `smallest` to infinity — not 0 — is what lets the first real component set it.
approaches.insight: The problem reduces to component sizes; a flood fill produces them in one linear pass. The only subtlety is aggregating correctly — seed the minimum to infinity so it can actually shrink.

approaches.name: Union-Find with Size Tracking (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The cleanest answer for a flat edge list. Union each edge, carry size on each root, then sweep roots for the smallest and largest.
hints: You only need sizes, never paths. What structure merges groups and tracks their sizes in near-constant time per edge?
Union-Find: union each edge's endpoints with path compression and union by rank, and add the merged sizes onto the surviving root.
After all unions, scan the labels; for each label that is its own root, its size is its component size. Take the min and max over roots of size ≥ 2.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each union and find is O(α(N)) — inverse Ackermann, effectively constant. E edges give O(E · α(N)); the final root sweep is O(N · α(N)). Space is O(N) for parent, rank, and size arrays.
approaches.explanation:
Union-Find is the natural fit when edges arrive as a list and you only care about group sizes.

**Building components.** Every label starts in its own set. For each edge `[u, v]`, `union(u, v)`: if their roots differ, attach one tree under the other and add the smaller component's size onto the surviving root. After all edges, two labels share a root exactly when an edge-path connects them, and each root's `size` is its component size.

**Path compression and union by rank.** A naïve `find` can walk an `O(N)` chain; compressing the path during `find` and attaching the shorter tree beneath the taller one keep each operation at `O(α(N))` — at most about 4 for any realistic input. The `find` loop is a `while`, never recursive, so even a long chain of merges cannot overflow the stack.

**Why size lives on the root.** When two sets merge, only the surviving root's `size` is updated. A non-root keeps whatever stale value it had before being absorbed, so you must read `size` only after confirming `find(x) == x`. Reading it at a non-root is the classic bug.

**Aggregating.** Sweep all labels; for each that is its own root with `size ≥ 2`, update `smallest` (seeded to infinity) and `largest` (seeded to 0). Because every label in an edge sits in a component of size ≥ 2, the filter mainly guards against any label you might have allocated but never connected. The bipartite labeling never enters the logic — `union` treats left and right labels identically.
approaches.insight: Carrying `size` on the root during merges means the answer is one root sweep away. Union-Find's near-constant operations make this the go-to for size/min/max/count over components when the input is an edge list.

pitfalls: Reading size at a non-root — returns a stale partial size.
Seeding smallest to 0 — it never updates downward.
Recursive find on a long chain — risks stack overflow; use the iterative loop.
Updating size on both roots during a merge — double counts.

commonMistakes: Reading the size array at a non-root node, which holds a stale value.
Seeding the smallest to 0 so it can never be lowered by a real component.
Counting isolated nodes as size-1 components when the problem excludes them.
Recursive find or DFS on a long chain, overflowing the call stack.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Reading size at a non-root
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When two sets merge, only the surviving root's size is updated; the absorbed node keeps its old size. Reading size[x] without checking find(x) == x returns a wrong, partial count.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
for i in range(1, total_nodes + 1):
    largest = max(largest, size[i])   # size[i] stale unless i is a root

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Seeding smallest to zero
commonMistakesDetailed.why: min(0, anything positive) is always 0, so the smallest never changes from its seed. The minimum must start above every possible size — infinity.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
int smallest = 0;
smallest = Math.min(smallest, size[i]);   // stuck at 0
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
int smallest = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
smallest = Math.min(smallest, size[i]);

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Recursive find on a long chain
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A component can be a chain of tens of thousands of nodes. A recursive find nests one frame per node and overflows the stack; an iterative loop keeps depth in the heap.

patternNote: Union-Find Component Sizing with Aggregation. Recognize it when an edge list defines groups and you need a size aggregate — min, max, count, or per-group value. Carry size on the root during merges, sweep roots once. The same skeleton powers Number of Connected Components, Journey to the Moon, and Roads and Libraries.
